gist: Opens the chapter presenting 'The Six Keys of Eudoxus', a first-person practical text: it describes the First Key (extraction of the seed and first purification to whiteness), the Second Key (philosophical sublimation of the Stone by the Secret Fire, ending in putrefaction), and the long Third Key (separation, purification and reunion of the three principles of 'our Mercury' by washing the earth with its own water), then defines the two kinds of compound and the Pontick Water. The chunk breaks off mid-passage.

notes.point: Chapter heading: 'The Six Keys of Eudoxus, Opening Into the Most Secret Philosophy'. The body is spoken by a first-person 'I' addressing 'you'; by the heading this is Eudoxus. Atwood does not speak in her own voice in this chunk.

The First Key opens the dark prisons in which the Sulphur is shut up; it extracts the seed out of the body and forms the Stone of the philosophers by conjoining spirit with body, i.e. sulphur with mercury.

Hermes is cited as demonstrating the First Key: in the caverns of the metals is hidden the Stone, venerable, bright, a sublime mind and an open sea; it contains a Spirit of sublime origin and is the Sea of the Wise, in which they angle for their mysterious Fish.

The operations of the three works are much alike, and the philosophers deliberately speak equivocally so that those without 'Lynx's eyes' go wrong and are lost in the labyrinth; when they seem to speak of one work they often treat of another.

In each work the Artist must dissolve the body with the spirit, cut off the Raven's head, whiten the Black and vivify the White; but it is properly in the First operation that he cuts off the head of the Black Dragon and the Raven. Hermes: 'What is born of the Crow is the beginning of this Art.'

By separating the black, foul, stinking fume of the Blackest Black, the astral, white, resplendent Stone is formed, which holds in its veins the blood of the Pelican. The First Key ends at this First Purification and shining whiteness.
The Second Key dissolves the compound of the Stone and begins the philosophical separation of the Elements, done only by raising the subtle and pure parts above the thick and terrestrial.

Whoever can sublime the Stone philosophically deserves the name philosopher, because he knows the Fire of the Wise, the only instrument of this sublimation. No philosopher has openly revealed this Secret Fire, the agent of all the Art's wonders.

One who cannot understand the Fire or recognize it by the characters used to describe it should stop and pray: its knowledge is more a gift of Heaven than a product of natural reasoning. Still he should read the philosophers, meditate and above all pray; every difficulty yields to Work, Meditation and Prayer.

Without sublimation, the conversion of the Elements and extraction of the Principles is impossible; this conversion (Earth to Water, Water to Air, Air to Fire) is the only way to prepare 'our Mercury'.

The Secret Fire dissolves the Stone naturally and without violence into Water in the great sea of the Wise, by a distillation made by the rays of the Sun and Moon. Thus the Stone, 'the vine of the Wise' according to Hermes, becomes their Wine, which by Art yields their rectified Water of Life and most sharp Vinegar.

The Stone's Elements can be dissolved only by this 'Nature wholly Divine', and perfect dissolution only follows a proportioned digestion and putrefaction, where the Second Key 'of the First Work' ends.

The Third Key contains a longer train of operations than all the others together. Because the Perfection of 'our Mercury' depends on it, philosophers say little; even the sincerest (Artefius, Trevisan, Flammel) passed over the Preparation of our Mercury in silence, and nearly all feigned instead of showing this longest and most important operation.
The speaker promises to enlarge on it more than others, or at least set in order what they treated confusedly; without inspiration of Heaven or a faithful friend one stays lost in the labyrinth.

The Third Key concerns the separation and purification of the Principles of our Mercury, achieved by perfect dissolution and glorification of the body from which it was born, and by intimate union of the soul with its body, the Spirit being the only tie of this conjunction. It ends in a new substance infinitely nobler than the first.

After the spring of living water has been drawn from the stone and the vine pressed into wine, the Artist must note that this apparently homogeneous water contains three substances and principles, Salt, Sulphur and Mercury, which are spirit, soul and body; they seem united but are far from it. When the Water (soul and spirit) is distilled off, the Body stays at the bottom like dead, black, dredgy earth, which is not to be despised, since nothing in 'our subject' is not good.

John Pontanus holds that the Stone's very superfluities become a true essence, that whoever separates anything from the subject knows nothing of philosophy, and that the whole compound is perfected by 'our Fire'. This corrects those who think purification means keeping the subtile and throwing away the heavy.

Hermes: its power is not integral until turned into earth. Fire and Sulphur are hidden in the centre of the Earth, which must be washed exactly with its own spirit to extract the Fixed Salt, the Blood of our Stone. This is the essential Mystery, completed only after convenient digestion and slow distillation.

Fire and water are contrary, yet the Artist must make peace between these enemies who radically love each other. Cosmopolite: being purged, they make Fire and Water friends in their earth which ascended with them. Hence: moisten the earth often with its water.

The body must be dissolved by the water and the Earth penetrated with its Humidity to be fit for generation. The Spirit is Eve, the Body Adam, to be joined for propagation; Hermes says Water is the strongest Nature, which surmounts and excites the fixed Nature in the Body.

The two substances, same nature but different genders, ascend together insensibly, leaving little faeces; soul, spirit and body finally appear inseparably united in a nobler Form, as different from the first liquid form as exactly rectified alcohol of wine 'actuated with its salt' differs from wine. This comparison is said to give precise knowledge of the Third Key.
'Our Water' is a living Spring issuing from the Stone by a natural miracle; Hermes says the water issuing from the Stone is first of all and the foundation of the Art.

Philosophers call this water wine, water of life, vinegar or oil according to its degree of preparation or its effects; it is properly the Vinegar of the Wise. Its distillation behaves like common vinegar: water and phlegm rise first, the oily substance, in which the water's efficacy lies, comes last.

The body must be dissolved entirely to extract all its humidity, which contains the precious ferment, the sulphur, balm of Nature and wonderful unguent; without it the blackness desired by all philosophers will never appear in the vessel.

Reduce the whole compound into water and perfectly unite volatile with fixed. Senior's precept: the highest fume is to be reduced to the lowest, for the divine water descends from heaven and reduces the soul to its body, which it at length revives.

The Balm of Life is hidden in the unclean faeces; wash them with the celestial water until their blackness is removed, and the Water will then be animated with the Fiery Essence that works all the Art's wonders.

Philosophers have two compounds. The compound of Nature (spoken of in the First Key) is made by Nature in a way incomprehensible to the Artist, who only lends Nature a hand by applying external things. The compound of Art is made by the Wise man through the secret union of fixed with volatile, with a prudence gained only from profound philosophy; it differs in the Second and Third Work but is always the Artist's making.
Geber defines the compound as a mixture of Argent vive and Sulphur, i.e. volatile and fixed, which act on one another and are reciprocally volatilized and fixed into perfect Fixity.
Nature's example: earth bears no fruit unless penetrated by its humidity, and humidity stays barren unless retained and fixed by the dryness of earth.

So in the Art: in the first work one must purify the Serpent born of the Slime of the earth and whiten the foul black faeces to separate the white sulphur, the Sal Amoniac of the Wise and their Chaste Diana bathing; the whole mystery is the extraction of the fixed salt of the compound, in which all the energy of our Mercury consists.

Water rising by distillation carries up part of this fiery salt, so repeated affusion of the water on the body impregnates, fattens and fertilizes our Mercury and makes it fit to be fixed, which is the end of the second Work. Hermes: seeing the water grow by degrees thicker and harder, he rejoiced, knowing he would find what he sought.

This viscous liquor is rightly called Pontick Water: its exuberant ponticity is the true mark of its virtue, which grows the more it is rectified and worked. It is called Water of Life because it gives life to the metals, but properly the great Lunaria for its shining brightness. The text breaks off with '....'.

method.veiled: opens the dark prisons in which the Sulphur is shut up
method.plain: The first operation releases the active principle (Sulphur) locked inside the body/matter, extracting its 'seed'.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶3: same sentence glosses it as that which 'knows how to extract the seed out of the body' and conjoins 'sulphur with mercury'.

method.veiled: forms the Stone of the philosophers by the conjunction of the spirit with the body -- of sulphur with mercury
method.plain: The Stone is first formed by joining spirit and body; the text equates this with joining sulphur and mercury.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶3, the dash gives the equivalent formulation.

method.veiled: In the caverns of the metals there is hidden the Stone, which is venerable, bright in colour, a mind sublime, and an open sea
method.plain: The Stone is hidden within 'the metals' and is described as bright, as containing a spirit of sublime origin, and as a 'sea' in which the wise seek their 'Fish'.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶3: Eudoxus's restatement 'it contains a Spirit of a sublime original; it is the Sea of the Wise'. What 'the metals' are is not stated.

method.veiled: the philosophers do designedly speak in equivocal terms, to the end that those who have not the Lynx's eyes may pursue wrong
method.plain: Texts deliberately blur which of the three analogous works they describe; a reader must sharply discriminate which work is meant.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶3: 'when one imagines that they speak of one work, they often treat of another'.

method.veiled: he must cut off the Raven's head, whiten the Black, and vivify the White
method.plain: A recurring sequence in each work: end the black stage, bring the matter to whiteness, then give life to the white.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶3: listed alongside 'dissolve the body with the spirit' as what happens 'in each work'; ¶3 ends with separation of the black fume yielding the white Stone.

method.veiled: it is properly in the First operation that the Wise Artist cuts off the head of the Black Dragon and of the Raven
method.plain: Removal of the blackness belongs chiefly to the first operation.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶3: followed by 'What is born of the Crow is the beginning of this Art' and by the separation of the 'Blackest Black' ending the First Key.

method.veiled: What is born of the Crow is the beginning of this Art
method.plain: The Art begins from what comes out of the black stage.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶3: Crow/Raven paired with 'the Black'; the white Stone is formed by separating the black fume.

method.veiled: by separation of the black, foul, and stinking fume of the Blackest Black that our astral, white, and resplendent Stone is formed, which contains in its veins the blood of the Pelican
method.plain: Separating off a black, foul vapour leaves a pure white shining Stone; the First Key ends with this first purification and whiteness.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶3: 'It is at this First Purification of the Stone, and at this shining whiteness, that the work of the First Key is ended.' 'Blood of the Pelican' is not explained.

method.veiled: this separation of the elements is not made but by raising up the subtle and pure parts above the thick and terrestrial parts
method.plain: The Second Key separates the elements by sublimation: lifting the fine, pure part above the coarse, earthy part.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶5, directly; next sentence calls it to 'sublime the Stone philosophically'.

method.veiled: the Fire of the Wise, which is the only instrument which can work this sublimation
method.plain: A special 'fire', never openly named, is the sole agent of the sublimation; it dissolves the Stone gently, without violence.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶5: 'this Secret Fire, which dissolves the Stone naturally and without violence'; 'this Nature wholly Divine'. Its identity is withheld in the text.

method.veiled: the knowledge of this great Secret is rather a gift of Heaven, than a Light acquired by the natural force of reasoning
method.plain: The operator should stop if he cannot recognize the Fire, and seek it by prayer, reading the philosophers, and meditation, since its knowledge comes more by grace than by reasoning.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶5: 'there is no difficulty which may not in the end be made clear by Work, Meditation, and Prayer.'

method.veiled: this conversion, which makes Water of Earth, Air of Water, and Fire of Air, is the only way whereby our Mercury can be prepared
method.plain: Preparing 'our Mercury' requires a stepwise conversion of the elements upward, which in turn requires the sublimation.

method.veiled: makes it dissolve into Water in the great sea of the Wise, by the distillation which is made by the rays of the Sun and Moon
method.plain: The Fire dissolves the Stone into a water; the distilling agent is figured as 'rays of the Sun and Moon'.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶5; what 'Sun and Moon' denote is not stated in the chunk.

method.veiled: the Stone, which, according to Hermes, is the vine of the Wise, becomes their Wine, which, by the operations of Art, produces their rectified Water of Life, and their most sharp Vinegar
method.plain: The dissolved Stone yields a liquid ('Wine'), which further work refines into 'Water of Life' and 'Vinegar'.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶5; ¶8 says these names mark degrees of preparation or effects of one water.

method.veiled: nor can a perfect dissolution be made of it, but after a proportioned digestion and putrefaction
method.plain: Full dissolution needs a measured period of digestion and putrefaction; this ends the Second Key.

method.veiled: the Preparation of our Mercury
method.plain: The Third Key, the longest and most important operation, prepares 'our Mercury'; authors conceal or feign it.

method.veiled: a perfect dissolution and glorification of the body, whence it had its nativity, and by the intimate union of the soul with its body, of whom the Spirit is the only tie
method.plain: The Third Key separates and purifies the principles by fully dissolving and exalting the original body, then reunites soul with body through the spirit as link, producing a nobler substance.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶7: 'terminate at the generation of a new substance infinitely nobler than the First'.

method.veiled: in this homogeneous substance, which appears under the form of Water, there are three different substances, and three natural principles of bodies --- Salt, Sulphur and Mercury --- which are the spirit, the soul, and the body
method.plain: The water obtained looks uniform but holds three principles not yet truly united.

method.veiled: the Body remains in the bottom of the vessel, like a dead, black, and dredgy earth, which, nevertheless, is not to be despised
method.plain: Distilling off the water (soul and spirit) leaves a black residue (body) which must be kept, not discarded.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶7, reinforced by Pontanus: 'he who pretends to separate anything from our subject knows nothing of philosophy'.

method.veiled: persuade themselves that they must only take the subtile and cast away the heavy
method.plain: Error: thinking purification means keeping only the fine part; the whole compound, dregs included, is perfected by 'our Fire'.

method.veiled: they must wash it exactly with its spirit, to extract out of it the Fixed Salt, which is the Blood of our Stone
method.plain: The residue ('Earth') is washed with its own distilled spirit to draw out the fixed salt; done through convenient digestion and slow distillation.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶7: 'the Fire and the Sulphur are hidden in the centre of the Earth'; 'not accomplished till after a convenient digestion and a slow distillation'.

method.veiled: moisten oftentimes the earth with its water, and you will obtain what you seek
method.plain: Repeatedly pour the distilled water back on its own residue (cohobation-like reiteration).
method.basis: IV.3 ¶7; ¶9 repeats: 'the affusion of the water on the body, reiterated many times'.

method.veiled: the Wise Artist must make peace between the enemies, who radically love each other vehemently
method.plain: Contraries (fire and water) must be reconciled; Cosmopolite says they become friends 'in their earth, which had ascended with them'.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶7: placed between the washing of the Earth with its spirit and 'moisten oftentimes the earth with its water', implying the reconciliation happens through that washing.

method.veiled: the Spirit is Eve, the Body is Adam; they ought to be joined together for the propagation of their species
method.plain: Spirit and body are a female/male pair that must be united for 'generation'.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶7: 'two substances, which are of the same nature but of different genders'.

method.veiled: ascend insensibly together, leaving but a little faeces in the bottom of their vessel
method.plain: Sign of success of the Third Key: spirit and body rise together leaving little residue, giving a united, nobler form, compared to rectified alcohol of wine with its salt versus wine.

method.veiled: Our Water is a living Spring which comes out of the Stone by a natural miracle of our philosophy
method.plain: The key liquid is drawn from the Stone itself; it is the foundation of the Art and is properly the 'Vinegar of the Wise'.

method.veiled: the water and the phlegm ascend first; the oily substance, in which the efficacy of the water consists, comes the last
method.plain: In distilling this liquor, the watery part comes first and the effective oily part last.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶8, by analogy with common vinegar.

method.veiled: this blackness so desired by all the philosophers
method.plain: A desired blackness in the vessel appears only if the body is wholly dissolved and all its humidity (the ferment/sulphur/balm) extracted.

method.veiled: the highest fume should be reduced to the lowest
method.plain: The volatile must be brought back down onto the fixed: the divine water 'descending from heaven' restores the soul to its body and revives it.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶8: 'make a perfect union of the volatile with the fixed'; 'the reducer of the soul to its body, which it at length revives'.

method.veiled: you ought to wash them with this celestial water until you have removed away the blackness from them
method.plain: Wash the black dregs with the water until they lose their blackness; the water then becomes charged with the 'Fiery Essence'.

method.veiled: who does nothing but lend a hand to Nature by the adhibition of external things
method.plain: For the compound of Nature the Artist only assists Nature by applying external things; the compound of Art he makes himself by uniting fixed and volatile, which requires profound philosophy.

method.veiled: which, acting on one another, are volatilized and fixed reciprocally into a perfect Fixity
method.plain: Volatile and fixed act on each other until both reach a stable fixed state; illustrated by earth and its moisture needing each other to bear fruit.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶9, Geber's definition and the 'example of Nature'.

method.veiled: purify the Serpent, born of the Slime of the earth
method.plain: In the first work, purify and whiten the black dregs to separate the white sulphur; this is the extraction of the fixed salt.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶9: 'all this mystery is but the extraction of the fixed salt of our compound'. What the 'Serpent' itself is, is not stated beyond this context.

method.veiled: the affusion of the water on the body, reiterated many times, impregnates, fattens, and fertilizes our Mercury, and makes it fit to be fixed
method.plain: Repeated pouring of the water on the body enriches the Mercury with the fiery salt the water carries up, readying it for fixation (end of the second Work).

method.veiled: the water by degrees did become thicker and harder
method.plain: Progressive thickening of the water is a sign of success; its viscosity ('ponticity') marks its virtue.
method.basis: IV.3 ¶9: 'Its exuberant ponticity is indeed the true character of its virtue'.

terms.meaning: One of six named stages of operation; the First ends at the first purification and whiteness, the Second at putrefaction, the Third (longest) at a new nobler substance from reunited principles.

quotes.text: The Third Key comprehends of itself alone a longer train of operations than all the rest together.

terms.meaning: There are three works, with analogous operations which philosophers deliberately confuse; the Keys are distributed among them.

makes it fit to be fixed, which is the end of the second Work

ambiguities.quote: at which the operation of the Second Key of the First Work is ended
readings: The first two Keys belong to the First Work, and the 'second Work' ending in ¶9 corresponds to a later Key (e.g. the Third).
'Work' is used loosely and the Keys-to-Works mapping is not consistent within the chunk.
ambiguities.basis: ¶5 places the Second Key in the First Work; ¶9 says purifying the Serpent and whitening faeces happens 'in the first work' and that repeated affusion making Mercury fit to be fixed is 'the end of the second Work'; ¶3 warns philosophers deliberately confuse the three works.

ambiguities.quote: Salt, Sulphur and Mercury --- which are the spirit, the soul, and the body
readings: Paired in order: Salt = spirit, Sulphur = soul, Mercury = body.
Only the set-level identity is asserted (three principles = spirit, soul, body), not one-to-one pairing.
ambiguities.basis: ¶7 lists both triads in sequence without explicit pairing; elsewhere in the chunk the Fixed Salt is extracted from the Earth/body (¶7, ¶9) and is 'the Blood of our Stone', which does not obviously fit Salt = spirit.

ambiguities.quote: by the distillation which is made by the rays of the Sun and Moon
readings: A figurative description of the Secret Fire's action.
Literal reference to solar and lunar influence in the distillation.
ambiguities.basis: ¶5 calls the Fire 'Nature wholly Divine' and says it works 'naturally and without violence'; the chunk gives no further gloss on Sun and Moon.

ambiguities.quote: In the caverns of the metals
readings: Literal metals as the place of the Stone.
'Metals' used in a veiled sense for the subject.
ambiguities.basis: ¶3 stresses equivocal language by design; ¶9 says the Water 'gives life to the metals'. The chunk does not define 'metals'.

threads.note: Chapter title announces six Keys; only the first three are described in this chunk (the Keys continue beyond it).
Refers to 'the three works' as analogous; later Keys/works will treat the Second and Third Work.
Eudoxus promises to 'enlarge' on the Third Key more than others have; the exposition continues past ¶7 into ¶8-¶9 and possibly the next chunk.
'the compound of Nature, whereof I have spoken in the First Key' points back to ¶3.
'The compound of Art is not altogether the same in the Second as in the Third Work' anticipates the Third Work's compound, not described here.
Chunk ends with '....' mid-discussion of the Pontick Water / great Lunaria; continuation expected in the next chunk.
